Desiccated

/DESS-ih-kay-tid/ - the stress falls on DESS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Desiccated means dried up, with the moisture removed.

The lunchbox came back from camp with one desiccated orange rattling around inside it like a maraca.

Worked Example

Every guitar that moves to the high desert fights the same war, and the Santa Fe repair shop keeps a shelf of the losers: tops split along the grain, bridges lifted, one mandolin whose back opened like a seed pod. Wood cut in humid lowlands carries water in every cell, and a winter of furnace air leaves it desiccated — not dry to the touch but dry all the way through, shrunken past the builder's numbers. The waiting room runs a humidifier the size of a stove.

Desiccated is the exact word for that wood, because it means dried up, with the moisture removed — removed being the working part. Dry names a state; desiccated reports a process finished, the water taken out of a thing's very tissue, which is why it suits old wood, forgotten fruit, and lab samples better than a sunny afternoon.

How Desiccated Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dried-out

dried-out: the plain phrase; desiccated adds "completely, clinically"

shriveled

shriveled: shrunken and wrinkled by the drying

Antonyms

moist

moist: still holding water

sodden

sodden: soaked right through

How Strong Is It? — dry → parched → desiccated

dry vs. desiccated

dry vs. desiccated: Dry is a state any towel reaches by evening — nothing to write home about.

parched vs. desiccated

parched vs. desiccated: Parched goes further than dry — cracked, gasping, drought-deep; desiccated claims the most: the water is gone from inside the thing, and no single rain puts it back.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of desiccated.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: thoroughly

Root — sicc-

Root — sicc-: dry (Latin siccus)

Suffix — -ated

Suffix — -ated: made into

Put it together

Put it together: De- (thoroughly) + sicc- (dry) + -ated = made thoroughly dry. Latin siccus was plain "dry," and desiccare meant to dry something out on purpose. Here the unit's prefix is the intensifier — nothing is reversed; the dryness is simply driven all the way in.

Why there's almost no relative to spot

Why there's almost no relative to spot: Latin siccus, "dry," survives in English almost nowhere — except the little packet marked desiccant that ships inside shoeboxes and camera bags, there to drink up moisture before it reaches the goods. Same family, same job; beyond that, the root's line ends here.

Strength Check

Word Choice

technical / vivid

Desiccated is the laboratory's and the archaeologist's word — reach for it when the drying is total and the point of the sentence. A dry summer, a parched lawn, a shriveled apple each keep their everyday word. Beside this unit's desolate, note what is missing in each: a desiccated thing has lost its water; a desolate place has lost its people.
